claim: Absence is a notion that is usually captured by language-related concepts like zero or negation.
source: Absence is a notion that is usually captured by language-related concepts like zero or negation.
evidence: This is a general statement about how absence is conceptualized, drawing from established understanding in cognitive science.

claim: Roughly four objects can be tracked and maintained in mind simultaneously, even when they are moving or are occasionally occluded.
source: Investigations targeting object cognition revealed that roughly four objects can be tracked and maintained in mind simultaneously, even when they are moving or are occasionally occluded (Kahneman et al., 1992; Scholl and Pylyshyn, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kahneman et al., 1992 and Scholl and Pylyshyn, 1999.

claim: The approximate number system provides imprecise representations of sets to pre- and nonlinguistic creatures.
source: Such encoding is performed by the approximate number system, which provides imprecise representations of sets to pre- and nonlinguistic creatures as well.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the approximate number system.

claim: Information in the approximate number system is only an approximation of the size of the set and it is sensitive to proportional rather than to absolute differences.
source: However, in contrast to the object tracking system, information in this number system is only an approximation of the size of the set and it is sensitive to proportional rather than to absolute differences (Dehaene, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dehaene, 1997.

claim: Both the object tracking system and the approximate number system emerge early in individual development.
source: Both systems emerge early in the individual development (Piazza, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Piazza, 2010.

claim: Both the object tracking system and the approximate number system are shared by several species including mosquito fish, domestic chicks, rhesus monkeys, and great apes.
source: and are shared by several species (e.g., mosquito fish, domestic chicks, rhesus monkeys, and great apes; Haun et al., 2011; Brannon and Merritt, 2011; Vallortigara, 2012; Brannon and Roitman, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haun et al., 2011; Brannon and Merritt, 2011; Vallortigara, 2012; Brannon and Roitman, 2003.

claim: Negation conveying absence emerges among the first linguistic expressions between 1 and 2 years of life in human children.
source: Negation conveying absence (e.g., 'all gone') emerges among the first linguistic expressions between 1 and 2 years of life (Bloom, 1970; Pea, 1980; Choi, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bloom, 1970; Pea, 1980; Choi, 1988.

claim: Preschoolers can flexibly use sentential negation to express the absence of something in a numerical context.
source: Some years later, preschoolers can flexibly use sentential negation to express the absence of something in a numerical context (Bialystok and Codd, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bialystok and Codd, 2000.

claim: Preschoolers can recruit complex numerical concepts, such as zero.
source: and can recruit complex numerical concepts, such as zero (Wellman and Miller, 1986; Merritt and Brannon, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wellman and Miller, 1986; Merritt and Brannon, 2013.

claim: Monkeys can integrate empty sets with other sets relying on the approximate number system.
source: Studies involving numerical tasks indicate that monkeys can integrate empty sets with other sets relying on the approximate number system (Biro and Matsuzawa, 2001; Merritt et al., 2009; Howard et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biro and Matsuzawa, 2001; Merritt et al., 2009; Howard et al., 2018.

claim: Comparisons including empty sets are subject to distance effects, characteristic to the approximate number system.
source: For instance, comparisons including empty sets are also subject to distance effects, characteristic to the approximate number system (the smaller the distance between two numerosities, the more errors the subjects make) Merritt et al., 2009.
evidence: Supported by citation to Merritt et al., 2009.

claim: Empty sets are represented in the number specific areas of the monkey brain.
source: Empty sets, similar to other numerosities, are represented in the number specific areas of the monkey brain (Macaca fuscata: Okuyama et al., 2015; Macaca mulatta: Ramirez-Cardenas et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Okuyama et al., 2015 and Ramirez-Cardenas et al., 2016.

claim: The chimpanzee Ai learned to use a symbol for zero.
source: Furthermore, an interesting finding suggests that Ai, the chimpanzee learned to use a symbol for zero (Biro and Matsuzawa, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biro and Matsuzawa, 2001.

claim: Ai's performance likely reflected a rather limited conceptual understanding of zero, as she did not show transfer effects when switching from cardinality judgments to ordering tasks.
source: However, Ai's performance likely reflected a rather limited conceptual understanding of zero, as she did not show transfer effects when switching from cardinality judgments to ordering tasks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Ai did not show transfer effects.

claim: Preschoolers and monkeys tend to fail to discriminate an empty set from one item.
source: Evidence pointing to the possibility that this system may not be appropriate for such encoding comes from studies with preschoolers (Merritt and Brannon, 2013) and monkeys Merritt et al., 2009 who tend to fail to discriminate an empty set from one item.
evidence: Supported by citations to Merritt and Brannon, 2013 and Merritt et al., 2009.

claim: Contrary concepts, like absence/presence might be available even for nonhuman animals.
source: Bermúdez, 2003 proposed that contrary concepts, like absence/presence might be available even for nonhuman animals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bermúdez, 2003.

claim: Various species are able to exploit the presence and absence of stimulus.
source: The availability of contrary concepts in pre- and nonlinguistic animals has not been targeted by researchers, nevertheless, extensive research cumulating for over a century suggests that various species are able to exploit the presence and absence of stimulus (Pearce, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pearce, 2011.

claim: In monkeys, presence-specific neurons were found to be active when the animal perceived the stimulus and also later when making a decision.
source: While presence-specific neurons were found to be active when the animal perceived the stimulus and also later when making a decision, absence-specific neurons showed activation only when the subject decided about absence.
evidence: This is based on findings from a study by Merten and Nieder, 2012, mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: In monkeys, absence-specific neurons showed activation only when the subject decided about absence.
source: While presence-specific neurons were found to be active when the animal perceived the stimulus and also later when making a decision, absence-specific neurons showed activation only when the subject decided about absence.
evidence: This is based on findings from a study by Merten and Nieder, 2012, mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Different processes are involved in encoding the presence and absence of a stimulus in monkeys.
source: This finding, besides providing evidence for forming some representations of absence in monkeys, points to the possibility that different processes are involved in encoding the presence and absence of a stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential activation patterns of presence-specific and absence-specific neurons.

claim: Pigeons display feature-positive biases in learning tasks.
source: Pigeons (Hearst, 1984; as well as human adults, Newman et al., 1980) display feature-positive biases in learning tasks.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hearst, 1984 and Newman et al., 1980.

claim: Pigeons learned relatively easily the relation between the presence of a stimulus and food, but they had difficulties with discovering a similar relation between the absence of a stimulus and food.
source: Pigeons learned relatively easily the relation between the presence of a stimulus and food, but they had difficulties with discovering a similar relation between the absence of a stimulus and food.
evidence: This is based on the feature-positive bias mentioned in the context of Hearst, 1984.

claim: Human infants automatically detect and keep in mind the presence of objects after occlusion.
source: In line with such asymmetries, human infants automatically detect and keep in mind the presence of objects after occlusion, while they seem to fail to do so with the absence of objects (Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wynn and Chiang, 2016 and Kaufman et al., 2003.

claim: Human infants seem to fail to automatically detect and keep in mind the absence of objects after occlusion.
source: In line with such asymmetries, human infants automatically detect and keep in mind the presence of objects after occlusion, while they seem to fail to do so with the absence of objects (Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wynn and Chiang, 2016 and Kaufman et al., 2003.

claim: 8-day-old chicks were tested in the study.
source: We investigated 8-day-old chicks' looking behavior in response to events violating expectations about the presence or absence of an object.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the subjects of the study.

claim: Chicks displayed an avian signature of novelty detection to violations of absence, namely a sex-dependent left-eye-bias.
source: Importantly, chicks displayed an avian signature of novelty detection to violations of absence, namely a sex-dependent left-eye-bias.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Follow-up experiments excluded accounts that would explain the left-eye bias by perceptual mismatch.
source: Follow-up experiments excluded accounts that would explain this bias by perceptual mismatch or by representing the object at different locations.
evidence: This is based on the results of Experiment 3.

claim: Follow-up experiments excluded accounts that would explain the left-eye bias by representing the object at different locations.
source: Follow-up experiments excluded accounts that would explain this bias by perceptual mismatch or by representing the object at different locations.
evidence: This is based on the results of Experiment 4.

claim: The ability to spontaneously form representations about the absence of objects likely belongs to the initial cognitive repertoire of vertebrate species.
source: These results suggest that the ability to spontaneously form representations about the absence of objects likely belongs to the initial cognitive repertoire of vertebrate species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings with young chicks.

claim: In Experiment 1, 27 chicks (13 females, 14 males) were tested.
source: In Experiment 1 (Encoding Presence), chicks (n = 27, 13 females, 14 males) watched as the object moved behind the screen till full occlusion
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and composition.

claim: In Experiment 2, 28 chicks (15 females, 13 males) were tested.
source: In Experiment 2 (Encoding Absence), the test trials started with the screen in a lowered position. A different group of chicks (n = 28, 15 females, 13 males) observed an object moving to the area behind the lowered screen
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and composition.

claim: A repeated measures design was used where each chick was presented with both the Expected and the Unexpected conditions.
source: We used a repeated measures design; thus, each chick was presented with both the Expected and the Unexpected conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Chicks' overall Looking Times were differently modulated as a function of the outcomes violating or confirming the chicks' expectations about the presence and the absence of the object in Experiments 1 and 2.
source: Chicks' overall Looking Times were differently modulated as a function of the outcomes violating or confirming the chicks' expectations about the presence and the absence of the object in Experiments 1 and 2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the ANOVA results showing a significant interaction between Experiment and Outcome.

claim: A 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA with Experiment, Outcome, and Sex as factors yielded a significant interaction between Experiment and Outcome (F1, 51 = 4.244, p = 0.045, ηp2 = 0.077).
source: A 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA with Experiment (Experiment 1: Encoding Presence vs. Experiment 2: Encoding Absence), Outcome (Expected vs. Unexpected), and Sex (Female vs. Male) as factors yielded a significant interaction between Experiment and Outcome (F1, 51 = 4.244, p = 0.045, ηp2 = 0.077) with no other effects (IBM SPSS Statistics 20).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1, chicks' looking behavior seemed to be in line with the prediction of longer looking times for unexpected outcomes.
source: In Experiment 1, chicks' looking behavior seemed to be in line with the prediction of longer looking times for unexpected outcomes (untransformed means: Unexpected Disappearance: M = 15.421; SD = 7.34; Expected Disappearance: M = 12.671, SD = 6.566; Scheffé test p = 0.078, η2 = 0.037)
evidence: This is based on the descriptive statistics and post-hoc test results.

claim: In Experiment 2, chicks did not show longer looking times for unexpected outcomes.
source: however, this was not the case for Experiment 2 (Unexpected Appearance: M = 12.906; SD = 8.409; Expected Appearance: M = 14.556, SD = 9.351; Scheffé test, p = 0.273, η2 = 0.008).
evidence: This is based on the descriptive statistics and post-hoc test results.

claim: Subjects looked longer to the Unexpected outcomes in Experiment 1 compared to Experiment 2.
source: Subjects looked longer to the Unexpected outcomes in Experiment 1 compared to Experiment 2 (Scheffé test, p = 0.028, d = 0.318).
evidence: This is based on the post-hoc test results.

claim: Human infants show longer looks to violations of presence but not to that of absence.
source: Human infants show similar looking patterns to such scenes (i.e., longer looks to violations of presence but not to that of absence; Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wynn and Chiang, 2016 and Kaufman et al., 2003.

claim: A 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA performed on the Lateralization Index revealed a significant Experiment by Outcome interaction (F1, 51 = 4.652, p = 0.036, ηp2 = 0.084).
source: A 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA performed on the Lateralization Index revealed a significant Experiment by Outcome interaction (F1, 51 = 4.652, p = 0.036, ηp2 = 0.084), with no other significant effects.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: In the Unexpected Outcome condition subjects displayed a greater left-eye bias in Experiment 2 compared to Experiment 1.
source: Pairwise comparisons revealed that in the Unexpected Outcome condition subjects displayed a greater left-eye bias in Experiment 2 (Encoding Absence, M = 0.193, SD = 0.517) compared to Experiment 1 (Encoding Presence, M = −0.138, SD = 0.459; Scheffé test, p = 0.023, d = 0.677).
evidence: This is based on the post-hoc test results.

claim: The Lateralization Index may be sensitive to violations of expectation regarding the absence of objects, but not regarding the presence of objects.
source: These data suggest that the Lateralization Index may be sensitive to violations of expectation regarding the absence of objects, but not regarding the presence of objects (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential patterns observed in Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: A positive Lateralization Index reflects a left-eye bias, which was previously linked to detecting novel outcomes.
source: A positive Lateralization Index reflects a left-eye bias, which was previously linked to detecting novel outcomes (Rogers and Anson, 1979; Dharmaretnam and Andrew, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rogers and Anson, 1979 and Dharmaretnam and Andrew, 1994.

claim: The left-eye bias found in response to the unexpected appearance of the object likely reflected the chicks' exploration and attempt of identification of the unexpectedly emerging 'new' item.
source: The left-eye bias, found in response to the unexpected appearance of the object, likely reflected the chicks' exploration, and attempt of identification of the unexpectedly emerging 'new' item.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed left-eye bias.

claim: In Experiment 3, 31 chicks (15 females, 16 males) were tested.
source: Experiment 3 (Absence vs. Perceptual Comparison) followed the procedure of Experiment 2. However, unlike in Experiment 2, each trial started with the screen in upright position preventing the chicks (n = 31, 15 females, 16 males) to see the space occluded by the screen at the beginning of the trial (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and composition.

claim: In Experiment 4, 22 chicks (9 females, 13 males) were tested.
source: Experiment 4 (Absence vs. Tracking) (n = 22, 9 females, 13 males) was the same as Experiment 3, except that in the Unexpected Appearance condition the target object that moved behind the screen and then left the scene was different from the object that appeared when the screen was lowered in the outcome phase (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and composition.

claim: A 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA with Experiment, Outcome, and Sex as factors showed a main effect of Outcome (F1, 49 = 4.29, p = 0.044, ηp2 = 0.081).
source: We analyzed the Lateralization Index of Experiments 3 and 4 with a 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA with Experiment, Outcome, and Sex as factors. There was a main effect of Outcome (F1, 49 = 4.29, p = 0.044, ηp2 = 0.081)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: More positive Lateralization Index values (more usage of the left eye) were observed in response to unexpected outcomes compared to expected outcomes.
source: revealing more positive values (more usage of the left eye) in response to unexpected outcomes (M = 0.087, SD = 0.5) compared to expected outcomes (M = −0.045, SD = 0.459), similar to Experiment 2.
evidence: This is based on the descriptive statistics from the ANOVA.

claim: A significant interaction was observed between Outcome and Sex (F1, 49 = 4.804, p = 0.033, ηp2 = 0.089).
source: Additionally, a significant interaction was observed between Outcome and Sex (F1, 49 = 4.804, p = 0.033, ηp2 = 0.089)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Females showed sensitivity to events violating their expectations regarding absence of entities.
source: indicating females' sensitivity to events violating their expectations regarding absence of entities (Unexpected Appearance, M = 0.189; SD = 0.5; Expected Appearance, M = −0.133, SD = 0.5; post hoc Scheffé test, p = 0.007, η2 = 0.095)
evidence: This is based on the post-hoc test results.

claim: Males showed no difference in Lateralization Index between unexpected and expected outcomes.
source: while males showed no such difference (Unexpected Appearance, M = −0.01; SD = 0.49; Expected Appearance, M = −0.005, SD = 0.377; post hoc Scheffé test, p = 0.918, η2 = 0.000).
evidence: This is based on the post-hoc test results.

claim: A 3 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA evaluating the Lateralization Index with Experiment, Outcome, and Sex as factors found a main effect of Outcome (F1, 75 = 6.273, p = 0.014, ηp2 = 0.077).
source: Next, we included in a 3 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA the three Experiments that targeted absence encoding (Experiments 2–4), evaluating the Lateralization Index with Experiment, Outcome, and Sex as factors (Figure 4). We found a main effect of Outcome (F1, 75 = 6.273, p = 0.014, ηp2 = 0.077)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: More positive Lateralization Index values (more usage of the left eye) were observed for the Unexpected Appearance outcomes compared to the Expected Appearance outcomes across Experiments 2-4.
source: reflecting more positive values (more usage of the left eye) for the Unexpected Appearance outcomes (M = 0.123, SD = 0.506) compared to the Expected Appearance (M = −0.048, SD = 0.498) outcomes.
evidence: This is based on the descriptive statistics from the ANOVA.

claim: There was a significant interaction between Outcome and Sex (F1, 75 = 4.157, p = 0.045, ηp2 = 0.053) in the analysis of Experiments 2-4.
source: There was also a significant interaction between Outcome and Sex (F1, 75 = 4.157, p = 0.045, ηp2 = 0.053).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Females were more sensitive to the difference between the outcomes, indicating females' sensitivity to events violating their expectations regarding absence of entities.
source: Post hoc Scheffé test revealed that females were more sensitive to the difference between the outcomes, indicating females' sensitivity to events violating their expectations regarding absence of entities (Unexpected Appearance, M = 0.177, SD = 0.509; Expected Appearance, M = −0.156, SD = 0.556, p = 0.003, η2 = 0.091).
evidence: This is based on the post-hoc test results.

claim: Males did not appear to discriminate between expected and unexpected outcomes.
source: In contrast, males did not appear to discriminate between expected (M = 0.029, SD = 0.402) and unexpected outcomes (M = 0.065, SD = 0.506, p = 0.738, η2 = 0.002).
evidence: This is based on the post-hoc test results.

claim: There was no interaction between Experiment and Outcome factors in the analysis of Experiments 2-4.
source: Importantly, there was no interaction between Experiment and Outcome factors (F1, 75 = 0.156, p = 0.856), suggesting that the effects were similar in all the three experiments targeting absence representation.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Female chicks showed a statistically significant left-eye bias when they were confronted with the appearance of an object at a location that should have been empty.
source: When comparing the Lateralization Index to chance level (0), female (t38 = 2.173, p = 0.036, d = 0.348) but not male chicks (t41 = 0.837, p = 0.407, d = 0.128) showed a statistically significant left-eye bias when they were confronted with the appearance of an object at a location that should have been empty.
evidence: This is based on one-sample t-tests comparing the Lateralization Index to zero.

claim: Male chicks did not show a statistically significant left-eye bias when they were confronted with the appearance of an object at a location that should have been empty.
source: When comparing the Lateralization Index to chance level (0), female (t38 = 2.173, p = 0.036, d = 0.348) but not male chicks (t41 = 0.837, p = 0.407, d = 0.128) showed a statistically significant left-eye bias when they were confronted with the appearance of an object at a location that should have been empty.
evidence: This is based on one-sample t-tests comparing the Lateralization Index to zero.

claim: The results point to a sex-dependent abstract representation of absence in chicks, which is not attributable to a perceptual mismatch nor to the expectation of the presence of the imprinted object at a different location.
source: These results together point to a sex-dependent abstract representation of absence in chicks, which is not attributable to a perceptual mismatch (Experiment 3) nor to the expectation of the presence of the imprinted object at a different location (Experiment 4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of Experiments 2-4.

claim: Human infants, as well as other primates and domestic chicks as young as 4–5 days, represent the presence and the location of an object or agent even if it is no longer directly perceivable for them.
source: Several studies have shown that human infants (Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003), as well as other primates (Amici et al., 2010) and even domestic chicks as young as 4–5 days (Vallortigara et al., 1998; Regolin et al., 2005; Chiandetti and Vallortigara, 2011), represent the presence and the location of an object or agent even if it is no longer directly perceivable for them.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The object tracking system can encode the presence of physical objects or animate agents at specific locations and survives their occlusion.
source: Such a feat was proposed to be achieved by creating and maintaining an object index (Scholl and Pylyshyn, 1999) or an object file (Kahneman et al., 1992), which is dynamically linked to the location of the object and survives its occlusion.
evidence: Supported by citations to Scholl and Pylyshyn, 1999 and Kahneman et al., 1992.

claim: The object tracking system seems to break down at representing the absence of objects.
source: While such a tracking system can encode the presence of physical objects or animate agents at specific locations, it seems to break down at representing their absence (Scholl and Pylyshyn, 1999; Cheries et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scholl and Pylyshyn, 1999 and Cheries et al., 2008.

claim: There is an asymmetry between the cognitive abilities to represent presence and absence.
source: Indeed, previous research indicates an asymmetry between these two cognitive abilities (Hearst, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hearst, 1991.

claim: Human adults and pigeons readily learn the relation between the presence of a stimulus and reinforcement.
source: While human adults (Newman et al., 1980) and pigeons (Hearst, 1984) readily learn the relation between the presence of a stimulus and reinforcement, they have difficulties with recognizing the relation between the absence of a stimulus and reinforcement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Newman et al., 1980 and Hearst, 1984.

claim: Human adults and pigeons have difficulties with recognizing the relation between the absence of a stimulus and reinforcement.
source: While human adults (Newman et al., 1980) and pigeons (Hearst, 1984) readily learn the relation between the presence of a stimulus and reinforcement, they have difficulties with recognizing the relation between the absence of a stimulus and reinforcement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Newman et al., 1980 and Hearst, 1984.

claim: Spontaneously representing the absence of an object seems to exceed human infants' abilities.
source: Furthermore, human infants show remarkable capacities of object representation (Carey, 2009), but spontaneously representing the absence of an object seems to exceed their abilities (Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wynn and Chiang, 2016 and Kaufman et al., 2003.

claim: Grasping absent entities likely exploits additional cognitive mechanisms that are beyond those recruited for representing presence.
source: Thus, grasping absent entities likely exploits additional cognitive mechanisms that are beyond those recruited for representing presence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the asymmetries observed in representing presence and absence.

claim: Similar to human infants, chicks' looking times toward expected and unexpected outcomes were differently modulated in experiments testing the representation of presence and absence of an object.
source: In Study 1, we found that, similar to human infants (Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003), chicks' looking times toward expected and unexpected outcomes were differently modulated in experiments testing the representation of presence and absence of an object.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Study 1.

claim: Looking time was not sensitive to possible violations of absence representations.
source: However, looking time similar to the observations of human experiments with infants (Wynn and Chiang, 2016; Kaufman et al., 2003) was not sensitive to possible violations of absence representations.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Study 1.

claim: The left-eye bias was selectively sensitive only to scenes involving an object unexpectedly appearing in three experiments.
source: This measurement was selectively sensitive only to scenes involving an object unexpectedly appearing (violating expectations about its absence) in three experiments.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Experiments 2-4.

claim: Sex-dependent evidence was found for young chicks' ability to represent the absence of an object in their eye usage in the three experiments targeting absence representation.
source: Thus, remarkably, we found sex-dependent evidence for young chicks' ability to represent the absence of an object in their eye usage in the three experiments targeting absence representation (Experiments 2–4).
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Experiments 2-4.

claim: The results of Experiment 3 ruled out the possibility that the left-eye bias was the result of a mismatch between information stored in perceptual memory and the outcome of the scene.
source: The results of Experiment 3 ruled out the possibility that the left-eye bias associated with the novelty of inspected stimuli was the result of a mismatch between information stored in perceptual memory and the outcome of the scene.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Experiment 3.

claim: Experiment 4 showed that preferential left-eye use was independent of tracking the approximate location of a specific object.
source: Experiment 4 showed that preferential left-eye use was independent of tracking the approximate location of a specific object.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Experiment 4.

claim: Chicks' representations of absence seem to involve complex mental computations and possibly complex representations, that go beyond the object tracking system.
source: Instead, chicks' representations of absence seem to involve complex mental computations and possibly complex representations, that go beyond the object tracking system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: Female chicks encode not only the presence but also the absence of objects in their environment.
source: Altogether, our findings support the conclusion that female chicks encode not only the presence but also the absence of objects in their environment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: The left-eye bias reflects chicks' attempt to identify a novel object that appeared at a location where 'nothing' was expected to be.
source: We propose that the left-eye bias reflects chicks' attempt to identify a novel object that appeared at a location where 'nothing' was expected to be.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed left-eye bias.

claim: Previous studies reporting left-eye bias in domestic chicks also involved objects as stimuli.
source: Previous studies reporting left-eye bias in domestic chicks (Rogers and Anson, 1979; Dharmaretnam and Andrew, 1994) also involved objects as stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rogers and Anson, 1979 and Dharmaretnam and Andrew, 1994.

claim: No former work found left-eye preference in domestic chicks without a physical object.
source: According to our knowledge, no former work found left-eye preference in domestic chicks without a physical object.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: The left-eye bias is closely connected to the perceptual processing of objects, which in this case were most likely social (imprinting) objects.
source: This suggests that this specific behavior is closely connected to the perceptual processing of objects, which in our case were most likely social (imprinting) objects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that left-eye bias was only found when objects were present.

claim: The left-eye bias was prominent in females compared to males.
source: Second, the left-eye bias was prominent in females compared to males, and such sex-dependent differences are congruent with findings in social discrimination experiments with chicks (Vallortigara et al., 1990Vallortigara and Versace, 2017; Vallortigara and Andrew, 1994; Versace et al., 2017; Pallante et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the experimental results and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Female chicks are more interested in familiar social partners, while males are more interested in unfamiliar ones.
source: Indeed, female chicks are more interested in familiar social partners, while males are more interested in unfamiliar ones (Vallortigara, 1992)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vallortigara, 1992.

claim: These preferences are also observed in experiments using artificial social partners and different sensory modalities.
source: and these preferences are also observed in experiments using artificial social partners (Vallortigara and Andrew, 1994) and different sensory modalities (Versace et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vallortigara and Andrew, 1994 and Versace et al., 2017.

claim: In natural populations adult fowls exhibit territorial behavior, wherein single dominant cocks maintain and patrol a large territory within which a number of females live.
source: Specifically, in natural populations adult fowls exhibit territorial behavior, wherein single dominant cocks maintain and patrol a large territory within which a number of females live, and this sort of social organization favors the prevalence of gregarious and affiliative behaviors in females (McBride and Foenander, 1962; Andrew, 1966).
evidence: Supported by citations to McBride and Foenander, 1962 and Andrew, 1966.

claim: Females are more inclined to use the right eye for a conspecific and the left eye for a novel stimulus.
source: Furthermore, females are more inclined to use the right eye for a conspecific and the left eye for a novel stimulus (Dharmaretnam and Andrew, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dharmaretnam and Andrew, 1994.

claim: 8-day-old chicks prefer to look at an approaching unfamiliar object using their left eye.
source: and 8-day-old chicks prefer to look at an approaching unfamiliar object using their left eye (Rogers and Anson, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rogers and Anson, 1979.

claim: Female chicks identified the unexpectedly appearing object as a novel, unfamiliar object, even when it looked identical to an object they were familiarized to.
source: Based on these previous findings, the most plausible explanation of the pattern observed in the present work is that female chicks identified the unexpectedly appearing object as a novel, unfamiliar object, even when it looked identical to an object they were familiarized (and, in fact, imprinted) to.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed behavior based on previous findings.

claim: The chicks attempted to reidentify the object despite its match to the imprinted perceptual profile, possibly because they deemed it unfamiliar as its presence at a location represented as empty contradicted their expectation.
source: Thus, the chicks attempted to reidentify the object despite its match to the imprinted perceptual profile, possibly because they deemed it unfamiliar as its presence at a location represented as empty contradicted their expectation — the absence of objects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed behavior.

claim: The left-eye bias observed in the present study is likely a signature of chicks' attempt to identify the unexpectedly appearing object, given that its presence contradicts their expectation of absence of objects.
